---
title: "Data Analysis in Life Sciences"
---

Learn how computers organise information, how to work in a Linux command line,
and how to use R to turn biological measurements into figures and reproducible
reports.

We start with files and folders. You do not need previous programming experience.
Each lesson combines an explanation, a worked example, and a practical where you
save something you can find and use again. The biology includes seedling growth,
photosynthesis, calibration measurements, and a small duckweed experiment.
Short transfer choices also use basic organic-laboratory records, such as the
percentage of a supplied maximum product mass collected. Each exercise explains
the required quantities and calculation; prior chemistry is not required.

::: {.callout-note}
All course datasets are simulated teaching data. They help us practise a workflow;
they are not evidence about actual biological effects.
:::

## Your five-week route

Each topic in the left menu has separate **Lecture (slides)** and
**Practical and notes** links. Lecture links are green; practicals are italic;
weekly quiz links are blue. Coloured week bands follow the Quantitative Biology
course scaffold. The labels identify their roles even without colour.

Use the [five-week study plan](study-plan.qmd) to organise the work. Each daily
practical includes **Extended practical** and **Independent transfer** blocks:
apply the taught ideas to a changed problem, save the result, explain it, and
reproduce it from a fresh start. These are core practice, with gradually fewer
prompts. Weekly self-checks and protected review/support time complete the plan.

| Week | Biological question | What you will do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1 — Files and computers](week1/01-files.qmd) | Where are the seedling measurements? | Save and find files, use a terminal, unpack ZIPs, and search lab records |
| [2 — R and reports](week2/06-r-basics.qmd) | How much did the seedlings grow? | Import a table, calculate growth, plot it, and render R Markdown |
| [3 — Variation](week3/11-data-quality.qmd) | How much do individual plants differ? | Check data, summarise groups, understand mean, variance, SD, and replication |
| [4 — Comparisons and lines](week4/16-comparisons.qmd) | How do treatments and measurements relate? | Interpret a t-test, handle pairs, fit a calibration line, and describe an association |
| [5 — Reproducibility](week5/21-remote-workflow.qmd) | Can someone repeat our analysis? | Work remotely, analyse another dataset, package a report, and test it in a fresh session |

## Getting started

- [Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal](intro/ubuntu-windows.qmd).
- [Install R and RStudio, then open your project](intro/r-rstudio.qmd).
- [Download the course project and laboratory archive](downloads/index.qmd).
- [Working on a remote Linux computer](intro/remote-linux.qmd).

Remote connection instructions will be added when the course environment is
confirmed. Installation help will be provided during the course.

Begin with [Day 1: save, find, and reopen a file](week1/01-files.qmd).
You can keep the [terminal reference](reference/terminal.qmd),
[R reference](reference/r.qmd), [statistics reference](reference/statistics.qmd),
and [glossary](reference/glossary.qmd) open while working. Using a reference is
part of the workflow, not a sign that you should have memorised everything.
